source.title: Hessian-based Analysis of Large Batch Training and Robustness to Adversaries
source.authors: Zhe-Wei Yao; A. Gholami; Qi Lei; K. Keutzer; Michael W. Mahoney

record.tranche_reason: Varies training batch size and reports train and test accuracy plus Hessian spectra, using a fixed training-loss target rather than the fixed epoch budgets specified by V5.
record.gate_note: The paper reports batch-size results in Tables 1, 2, and 7. It also reports adversarial robustness and Hessian measurements, but these do not test the claim versions about natural-label generalization conditions or magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.test_reason: The study measures batch-size effects on held-out accuracy, bearing on V5, but usually stops at a common training-loss target rather than a fixed epoch budget. Its results therefore cannot directly establish V5's fixed-budget prediction.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors emphasize that large batches tend toward higher weight-Hessian spectra and greater adversarial vulnerability, while robust training favors lower spectra. Clean-accuracy effects vary across settings, and they explicitly treat robust training as a preliminary possibility rather than an established solution to large-batch training.
record.recipe_differences: Varies batch size and measures train/test accuracy, but trains to a target loss rather than using a fixed epoch budget. The paper reports no weight decay or dropout in the batch-size experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size changes test accuracy and the Hessian spectrum; effects vary by architecture and dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger batches have higher unnormalized weight-Hessian spectra and greater vulnerability to adversarial inputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Batch size affects local weight curvature and adversarial robustness; this does not measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness or V5's clean held-out accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Adversarial training lowers weight-Hessian spectra and improves adversarial accuracy, sometimes reducing clean accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Robust training changes curvature and robustness, with dataset-dependent clean-accuracy costs.

record.problems: The batch-size sweep is trained to a training-loss target, not a fixed epoch budget. The paper says experiments were repeated at least three times and findings were consistent, but reports no uncertainty estimates for the tabulated accuracy values. Its large-batch robust-optimization comparison is described as preliminary and needing more extensive tests.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out from the natural-label batch-size accuracy tables. Hessian eigenvalues and adversarial-attack accuracies are not included because the versions do not name those measures as tests of the stated claim.

untested.parts: No original random-label experiments or natural-label versus random-label comparison.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold experiment.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparison.

The main accuracy sweeps do not hold epochs fixed. Table 8 does not specify enough budget and schedule details to establish a fixed-budget comparison. Language models, longer-training interventions, warmup, and normalization or regularization interventions are not tested.
No magnitude-scaled perturbation-tolerance measure or comparison of its ranking with norm- and margin-based measures.

missing.what: Table 8 reports C1 large-batch baseline accuracies of 75.59%, 75.61%, 70.23%, and 55.23% at batches 8000, 10000, 25000, and 50000. Corresponding learning-rate-scaled accuracies are 75.2%, 10%, 10%, and 10%; robust-training accuracies are 76.12%, 75.97%, 74.09%, and 71.16%. These results were neither extracted nor declared omitted.

record.verdict_notes: All recorded accuracy values match the supplied tables. Training accuracy near 100% together with lower test accuracy is not itself evidence of a batch-size penalty. Row states describe explicit within-architecture comparisons; none establishes the fixed-epoch condition. Experiments were reportedly repeated at least three times, but the accuracy tables contain no uncertainty estimates.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of random-label and natural-label test performance.
No convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison.

The study varies batch size and reports natural-label test accuracy, but trains until a target training loss rather than holding the number of epochs fixed. It does not test the language-model setting or the recipe adaptations listed in the version.
The study measures Hessian spectra but does not measure magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or compare it with norm- and margin-based measures.

relationships.condition: C1 and C2 on CIFAR-10, small-to-moderate batches, trained to a common loss target
relationships.reason: R1–R12 show nonmonotonic accuracy: batch 512 outperforms each architecture's smallest reported batch; these results require a workload-dependent threshold and do not establish a fixed-epoch effect.
relationships.display_finding: Batch 512 outperformed each CIFAR-10 architecture's smallest tested batch under loss-target stopping, leaving fixed-epoch effects untested.

relation.reason: The study reports its own batch-size sweeps and clean training/test accuracies, rather than only citing or using the finding.

tranche.reason: Direct batch-size comparisons measure held-out accuracy using loss-target stopping and Hessian analysis; this is a different method bearing on the same batch-size question.

source_check.notes: The batch-size rows use loss-target stopping, so their states describe accuracy comparisons rather than a demonstrated fixed-epoch effect. The authors report at least three repetitions, but the relevant accuracy tables provide no uncertainty estimates; Table 8 remains preliminary.
